demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
# Maya

Maya sits in the salon chair between appointments, her fingers working through a client's hair with practiced efficiency, though her movements feel mechanical today. At nineteen, she's been styling hair for just over a year—a job she once loved. She'd watched her mother work as a hairdresser her entire childhood and had dreamed of joining her in the family business. But that was before the accident.

It happened on a Tuesday afternoon, seven months ago. Maya was doing a keratin treatment for a regular client, Mrs. Chen, who'd been coming to the salon for years. The process requires careful application of chemical solution, precise timing, and steady hands. Maya had done it dozens of times. But that day, she was distracted—her mind half on her boyfriend, half on a text she'd received. As she smoothed the hot flat iron through Mrs. Chen's hair, the tool slipped. The ceramic plates caught the side of Mrs. Chen's neck and shoulder, causing a severe burn that required emergency room treatment and left permanent scarring.

The moment it happened, Maya's world fractured. Mrs. Chen's cry, the smell of burnt skin, the way the woman's hand flew to her neck—these images loop through Maya's mind without warning. They come at work, at home, in the middle of conversations with her boyfriend. She'll be blow-drying someone's hair and suddenly her hands will start shaking so badly she has to set down the dryer and excuse herself to the bathroom.

Since the accident, Maya has developed an almost obsessive checking ritual. Before every service, she tests the flat iron on her own wrist multiple times, even though logically she knows it works. She checks the temperature settings repeatedly, sometimes five or six times in a row, watching the digital display as if it might spontaneously change. Her manager has noticed but hasn't said anything. Her coworkers have noticed too—the way she's become quieter, more withdrawn, how she sometimes spaces out while clients are talking to her.

Sleep has become difficult. Maya lies awake at night, her mind replaying the accident in vivid detail, sometimes imagining worse outcomes. When she does sleep, she has nightmares where she's caused injuries to multiple people, where she's lost control of tools in her hands. She wakes up gasping, her heart racing. Her boyfriend has mentioned that she sometimes thrashes in bed, and once she accidentally hit him while dreaming.

Loud noises startle her intensely—the sound of the salon's blow dryers makes her jump, her whole body tensing. She's begun avoiding certain tasks, asking other stylists to do keratin treatments or anything involving heated tools. She's also started avoiding Mrs. Chen's salon visits, calling in sick on days the woman has an appointment, even though Mrs. Chen has tried to reach out to her, sending messages saying she doesn't blame her, that it was an accident.

Maya knows intellectually that what happened was an accident, that her hands slipped, that she didn't intentionally hurt anyone. But knowing this and believing it are different things. She feels fundamentally unsafe in her own body, unable to trust her hands to do what they're supposed to do. The job she once loved now feels like a minefield. Every client in her chair represents a potential for catastrophe. She's started wondering if she should find different work entirely, maybe something that doesn't involve tools or the possibility of harming someone. But the thought of leaving the salon feels like admitting defeat, like confirming that she's broken something in herself that can't be fixed.
